name: std::indirectly_unary_invocable, std::indirectly_regular_unary_invocable

declarations.code:
template <class F, class I>

concept indirectly_unary_invocable =

    std::indirectly_readable<I> &&

    std::copy_constructible<F> &&

    std::invocable<F &, /*indirect-value-t*/<I>> &&

    std::invocable<F &, std::iter_reference_t<I>> &&

    std::common_reference_with<

        std::invoke_result_t<F &, /*indirect-value-t*/<I>>,

        std::invoke_result_t<F &, std::iter_reference_t<I>>>;

template <class F, class I>

concept indirectly_regular_unary_invocable =

    std::indirectly_readable<I> &&

    std::copy_constructible<F> &&

    std::regular_invocable<F &, /*indirect-value-t*/<I>> &&

    std::regular_invocable<F &, std::iter_reference_t<I>> &&

    std::common_reference_with<

        std::invoke_result_t<F &, /*indirect-value-t*/<I>>,

        std::invoke_result_t<F &, std::iter_reference_t<I>>>;

intro: The concepts indirectly_unary_invocable and indirectly_regular_unary_invocable specify requirements for algorithms that call (regular) unary invocables as their arguments. The key difference between these concepts and std::invocable is that they are applied to the type the I references, rather than I itself.

sections.title: Notes
sections.text: The distinction between indirectly_unary_invocable and indirectly_regular_unary_invocable is purely semantic.
